title: Fragile Topology is Unstable Under Translation Refinement
authors: Yoonseok Hwang, Saavanth Velury, Taylor L. Hughes
abstract: Fragile topological phases become trivial upon the addition of suitable trivial bands, distinguishing them from stable topological phases. Nevertheless, various response phenomena and material realizations have been proposed for fragile phases. At the same time, many of these phenomena can also occur in atomic insulators, leaving open the question of what properties are specific to fragile phases. Enlarging the unit cell offers a natural perspective on this question. Band folding increases the number of bands in a manner analogous to adding trivial bands. In this work, we establish a systematic framework for determining the stability of fragile topology under unit-cell enlargement. We first establish a systematic criterion for trivialization under enlargements compatible with space-group symmetry, grounded in a physical electron-positron picture and formulated through a Hilbert-basis analysis of momentum-space symmetry data. We then show that, for all two-dimensional wallpaper groups, with or without spin-orbit coupling and/or time-reversal symmetry, every symmetry-indicated fragile phase is adiabatically connected to an atomic insulator in a suitable finite supercell and can therefore be trivialized by an arbitrarily small symmetry-preserving perturbation. Our results reveal that fragile topology has only finite stability under translation-symmetry refinement. This highlights that the fate of a fragile phase can depend on translation-symmetry-breaking perturbations, such as charge-density-wave ordering, and suggests that physical signatures insensitive to translation refinement are unlikely to uniquely characterize fragile topology.
summary: This theoretical work rigorously proves that 'fragile topology' is not fundamentally stable against lattice refinement. By analyzing symmetry-protected band structures using momentum-space data, the authors demonstrate that increasing the unit cell size (supercell construction) allows for an adiabatic deformation that trivializes the topological phase into a simple atomic insulator.
main_problem: The paper investigates the stability of 'fragile topological phases' under lattice enlargement (unit-cell refinement), aiming to distinguish them from stable topological phases or trivial atomic insulators.
main_result: It establishes that fragile topology possesses only finite stability, as all such phases can be shown to become adiabatically connected to an atomic insulator through a sufficiently large supercell enlargement ($N_{sc}=4$ in one example).
method: The analysis uses a systematic framework involving Hilbert-basis analysis of momentum-space symmetry data ($\mathbf{v} = 	ext{BR} \cdot \mathbf{m}$) and models unit-cell enlargement as an integer linear map to track the trivialization of topological invariants.
model_or_system: The study is applied to crystalline band topology, specifically analyzing 2D wallpaper groups using a tight-binding model framework derived from Wannier orbitals in an electron-positron picture.
key_observables: Symmetry-data vectors ($\mathbf{v}$), multiplicity vectors ($\mathbf{m}$), and the Wilson-loop spectrum $\{	heta_a(\mathbf{k})\}$ are key diagnostics for topological characterization and trivialization.
important_parameters: The supercell index ($N_{sc}$) is a critical parameter, as increasing it can drive the system toward a trivial state. The symmetry group (e.g., $p2$, $p4mm$) dictates the specific mathematical constraints.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that adiabatic deformations preserve both wallpaper-group symmetry and the bulk energy gap, allowing for the systematic tracking of topological invariants via symmetry data.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate Wyckoff positions, Brillouin zones with high-symmetry momenta, electron-positron configurations showing pair annihilation (trivialization), and supercell structures demonstrating band folding upon enlargement.
paper_structure: The paper develops from establishing the general instability criterion for fragile topology under unit-cell enlargement to providing detailed mathematical machinery using symmetry data vectors. It then applies this framework to specific 2D wallpaper groups, culminating in explicit calculations showing trivialization at finite supercell sizes.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter band theory rather than quantum information protocols, the rigorous mathematical tools developed for tracking topological stability under lattice changes (analogous to Hamiltonian perturbations) are highly relevant to understanding robustness in engineered quantum systems.
